strings.name: Liu Cixin
strings.role: Science fiction writer · Cosmic scales and civilizations
strings.summary: Liu wrote science fiction while working as a power-plant engineer, building stories from technical speculation, vast timescales and civilizational dilemmas. The Wandering Earth, Ball Lightning and the Three-Body trilogy turn scientific ideas into popular narratives. The Three-Body Problem won the 2015 Hugo, broadening Chinese science fiction’s international reach. He continues discussing adaptation, AI and imagination while distinguishing fictional strategies from real-world laws.
strings.coverageNote: Research cutoff: 2026-11-13. Selected milestones span 1963–2026; this is not a complete catalogue or live news archive.
strings.influence.rationale: Expanded the global readership of Chinese science fiction through the Three-Body trilogy, using cosmic-scale narratives to explore science, civilization and the future.
strings.facts.fact-01.label: Birthplace and upbringing
strings.facts.fact-01.value: Born in Beijing; raised in Yangquan, Shanxi
strings.facts.fact-02.label: Education
strings.facts.fact-02.value: Graduated from the hydropower engineering department of North China Institute of Water Conservancy and Hydroelectric Power in 1985
strings.highlights.highlight-01.title: The international reach of Three-Body
strings.highlights.highlight-01.text: Ken Liu’s English translation of The Three-Body Problem won the 2015 Hugo for Best Novel, bringing Chinese science fiction to broader global audiences.
strings.highlights.highlight-02.title: Scientific speculation as popular narrative
strings.highlights.highlight-02.text: From The Wandering Earth to Three-Body, engineering, physics and civilization’s fate connect across expansive fictional timescales.
strings.timeline.event-01.title: Reflects on twenty years of Three-Body
strings.timeline.event-01.text: In a People’s Daily interview he discussed imagination, adaptation and AI, describing continuing attempts to develop different fictional subjects.
strings.timeline.event-02.title: The Three-Body Problem wins the Hugo
strings.timeline.event-02.text: Ken Liu’s English translation won Best Novel, marking a significant moment for Chinese science fiction’s international recognition and readership.
strings.timeline.event-03.title: Publishes Death’s End
strings.timeline.event-03.text: The third Three-Body volume extended relations between humanity and cosmic civilizations across even larger scales of time and space.
strings.timeline.event-04.title: Publishes The Dark Forest
strings.timeline.event-04.text: The second volume develops strategies, deterrence and individual choices in humanity’s confrontation with an extraterrestrial civilization.
strings.timeline.event-05.title: The Three-Body Problem begins serialization
strings.timeline.event-05.text: Serialization in Science Fiction World connected scientists, historical memory and alien contact with questions at civilizational scale.
strings.timeline.event-06.title: Publishes Ball Lightning
strings.timeline.event-06.text: A scientific mystery becomes a novel interweaving research, military technology and personal obsession.
strings.timeline.event-07.title: Publishes The Wandering Earth
strings.timeline.event-07.text: A solar crisis forces Earth to begin an interstellar journey, linking engineering speculation with humanity’s collective fate.
strings.timeline.event-08.title: Publishes in Science Fiction World
strings.timeline.event-08.text: Whale Song and The End of the Microcosmos reached readers; Bring Her Eyes won a Galaxy Award that year.
strings.timeline.event-09.title: Graduates and begins power-plant work
strings.timeline.event-09.text: After engineering study he became a computer engineer at Niangziguan power plant in Shanxi, continuing fiction in his spare time.
strings.timeline.event-10.title: Born in Beijing
strings.timeline.event-10.text: Born in Beijing and raised in Yangquan, Shanxi; early science-fiction reading and interest in space travel informed his later writing.
